## business-model / 04_unit-economics.md

_Source: `business-model/04_unit-economics.md`_

# Unit Economics — EMAR

*Emaar Properties PJSC (DFM: EMAAR). UAE / Dubai issuer, IFRS, reporting currency AED, fiscal year = calendar year. Dominant segment taken from `03_segment-map.md`: Real Estate (build-and-sell developer), 79.8% of FY2025 revenue and 74.9% of segment profit. All figures below are sourced; derived ratios show their arithmetic so the reader can check them. USD conversions are the company's own stated equivalents from its press releases.*

## 1. Natural Unit

**The natural economic unit for the Real Estate segment is one residential unit (a home — apartment or villa) sold off-plan in a master-planned community, built and sold by the UAE build-to-sell business (Emaar Development).** "Off-plan" means the buyer signs up and pays in instalments while the home is still being built — this funding feature is central to the unit economics below.

The two smaller recurring segments have their own units — for **Leasing/Retail** it is one square foot of mall/commercial lettable area (GLA), and for **Hospitality** it is one hotel room (key). They are named here for completeness; the table is built for the dominant home-sale unit.

## 2. Unit Economics Table

| Unit Economic | Value | Period | Direction vs Prior Year | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue per unit (contracted sales value / ASP) | **~AED 3.87m per home (derived)** — UAE development pipeline of 47,000+ units carried a total contracted value of AED 182bn, 94% of it already sold [AED 182,000m ÷ 47,000 = AED 3.87m]. A separate ultra-luxury master plan (Emaar Hills JV) implies ~AED 2.5m/unit [AED 100bn ÷ 40,000]. A clean single-year average selling price (ASP) is not separately disclosed. | Q3/9M 2025 pipeline | **Improving** — management says launches took "increased prices… no pressure on pricing"; 48 launches at 90–100% absorption | Q3 FY2025 earnings call summary (FABS), 10 Nov 2025; Q4 FY2025 earnings call summary (FABS), 16 Feb 2026 |
| Gross margin per unit | **49.2%** on residential units [revenue AED 37,346.5m − cost AED 18,965.7m = AED 18,380.9m gross profit] — i.e. ~AED 49 of gross profit on each AED 100 of home revenue | FY2025 | **Stable / slightly down** (FY2024: 50.5% = 12,616.9 / 24,967.8); management guides gross margin "low 50s sustainably over the medium term" | FY2025 Annual Report (IFRS), Note 4 — Revenue, p.189 & Note 5 — Cost of Revenue, p.190; Q4 FY2025 earnings call summary (FABS) |
| Contribution margin per unit (after variable costs) | **~45% (derived)** — residential gross margin ~49% less the variable selling load: ~4% broker commission + sales & marketing of AED 1,569.5m (≈2% of AED 80.4bn property sales). This matches the segment operating margin of ~45% once the ~AED 2.77bn of finance income is stripped out (per segment-map). | FY2025 | **Stable** | Q3 FY2025 call summary (4% commission); FY2025 Annual Report, Note 6 — SG&A, p.190; `03_segment-map.md` |
| Cost to acquire / build the unit | **Acquire the sale: ~4% broker commission + ~2% sales & marketing ≈ ~6% of unit value.** Build the home: cost of residential units AED 18,965.7m in aggregate (recognised on percentage-of-completion; a per-home construction cost is **not disclosed**). Land embedded in the unit: land held for future development carried at ~**AED 81/sq ft** [AED 50,235.5m ÷ ~618m sq ft land bank]. | FY2025 / Q3 2025 | **Land cost rising** — 36m sq ft acquired in 2025 with AED 120bn gross development value | Q3 FY2025 call summary (4% commission); FY2025 Annual Report, Notes 5 & 6; CIQ Financials→Industry Specific, annual FY2025 (land held); Q4 FY2025 call summary (land buy) |
| Payback period / unit lifetime | **A one-time sale, recognised over ~4–5 years of construction, and largely pre-funded by the buyer.** Backlog of AED 155bn (unsatisfied sale obligations AED 174,883m) is expected to convert to revenue over ~5 years. Buyer instalments do most of the funding: advances from customers stood at AED 40,724m (2024: 32,495m), with AED 55,374m of new advances taken in during 2025 against AED 47,232m of revenue recognised, and ~AED 44bn sat in project escrow. So the developer's own cash outlay per home is recovered at or before completion (the business runs on negative working capital). Emaar Development physically delivered 6,129 homes in 2025. | FY2025 | **Improving** — advances +25% YoY; backlog +39% YoY | FY2025 Annual Report, Note 22 — Advances from Customers; FY2025 results press release, 12 Feb 2026; Q3 FY2025 call summary (escrow); Q4 FY2025 call summary (6,129 delivered) |

## 3. Value Creation Read

**Creates value — but at peak-cycle returns.** Each home carries a contribution margin of ~45% on a ~AED 3.9m unit and is largely paid for by the buyer during construction (advances of AED 40.7bn, ~AED 44bn in escrow), so the cash Emaar itself risks per unit is small and is recovered at or before handover. A one-time sale earning ~45% on minimal tied-up capital clears the value-creation bar comfortably — contribution far exceeds the ~6%-of-value cost to win and the modest own-capital cost to build. The math can be done, so this is not a data-gap case.

Ring-fence the read: **2025 was the top of the Dubai cycle**, not a normal year — the emirate saw a record ~270,000 transactions worth AED 892bn, and Emaar's own group return on capital (ROIC — profit earned on each AED of capital) rose to 12.5% in FY2025 (13.7% LTM) from 4.7% in FY2021 [CIQ Financials→Ratios / `ciq_facts.json`]. The 49% residential gross margin is elevated but **below the ~59% 2023 peak**, and the through-cycle range is wide: residential gross margin was ~32% in the 2020–21 trough, ~40% in 2022, ~59% in 2023, ~50% in 2024, ~49% in 2025 [CIQ Financials→Industry Specific, annual FY2020–FY2025]. Even at the ~32% trough margin, with the build pre-funded by buyers, the unit still creates value — just at a much lower return on capital. So: strongly value-creating at peak, still positive at trough. The single most valuable missing disclosure is a **clean annual figure for homes sold and their average contracted price (ASP) each year** — the company reports value aggregates (property sales, backlog) and cumulative unit counts (189,200+ sold since 2002), but not a per-year price per home, so the ASP above has to be inferred from pipeline value ÷ pipeline unit count.

## 4. Sensitivity

The read swings most on **price per home (ASP)**, and that is also the input with the most history of moving. Roughly 90%+ of the unit's economics ride on the Dubai off-plan price: land and construction costs are largely fixed once committed, so a 20% fall in ASP would compress the ~49% gross margin by far more than 20 percentage points, and would simultaneously slow the 90–100% absorption and the buyer pre-funding that make the model capital-light — a double hit to both margin and the negative-working-capital advantage. Price is not a hypothetical lever: residential gross margin has already swung from ~32% (2020–21) to ~59% (2023) to ~49% (2025), a range driven mainly by the Dubai price cycle. By contrast, the cost to acquire the sale (~4% commission + ~2% marketing) is small and steady — a 20% move there barely touches the conclusion — and construction cost, while the second-most-important lever, has been less volatile than price. Net: the whole unit-economics case is, at its core, a bet on the Dubai residential price cycle.

## business-model / 05_customer-geography.md

_Source: `business-model/05_customer-geography.md`_

# Customer And Geography Map — EMAR

**Company:** Emaar Properties PJSC (DFM: EMAAR) — Dubai (UAE) real-estate developer.
**Reporting standard:** IFRS. **Currency:** AED (UAE dirham, pegged to the US dollar at ~3.6725). US$ figures below are the company's own stated equivalents. Figures are FY2025 (year ended 31 Dec 2025) unless noted.

**Note on the CIQ "Customers" workbook:** the pool file `...EMAAR Customers.xls` is a Capital IQ *relationships* list — Emaar's own subsidiaries, intra-group borrowers, and two mall tenants (e.g. Jamjoom Fashion). It is **not** a customer-concentration disclosure, and I do not treat it as one. The real customer read comes from the audited credit-risk note and the segment note.

---

## 1. Customer Map

Emaar discloses **no individual customer and no top-customer concentration**. Its audited credit-risk note states the Group "earns its revenues from a **large number of customers spread across different geographies**" [FY2025 Annual Report (IFRS), Note 34(a) — Credit risk, p.213]. The table below is therefore a customer-**type** map, built from the three disclosed operating segments — each segment is effectively one customer type.

| Customer Type | Importance (% of revenue if disclosed) | Long-term Contract? (Y/N/Not disclosed) | Evidence | Risk |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Off-plan property buyers** (individuals & investors) — *Real Estate* segment | **~80%** (AED 39,550m of AED 49,557m) | **Y** — per-buyer Sale & Purchase Agreements on an instalment basis; 89% of group revenue is recognised "over a period of time" (booked as construction progresses, IFRS 15); AED 155bn contracted revenue backlog. Legal title passes only after all instalments are paid. | [FY2025 AR, Segment note, p.187–188; Note 34(a), p.213; Q4 FY2025 Earnings Press Release, 12-Feb-2026] | Granular base — customer default rate 0.5% of sales value [FY2025 AR, UAE Development, p.23]. Real risk is **market demand**, not any single buyer. |
| **Mall & retail tenants** (retailers) — *Leasing, Retail & Related Activities* segment | **~15%** (AED 7,681m) | **Y** — tenant lease agreements (lease income); 3,500+ retail units across the portfolio (Dubai Mall is the anchor). Per-tenant lease terms not disclosed. | [FY2025 AR, Segment note, p.187–188; AR p.23] | No single tenant disclosed as material; earnings tied to Dubai Mall footfall/occupancy. |
| **Hotel guests & leisure visitors** — *Hospitality* segment | **~5%** (AED 2,326m) | **N** — transactional stays/visits, recognised "point in time." | [FY2025 AR, Segment note, p.187–188] | Cyclical/tourism-linked; highly granular. |

**No single customer is disclosed at any material share of revenue.** The company's own framing: revenues come from "a large number of customers," and it maintains "specific guidelines to focus on the maintenance of a diversified portfolio... Identified concentrations of credit risks are controlled and managed accordingly" [FY2025 AR, Note 34(a), p.214].

---

## 2. Geography Map

The audited segment note splits geography only two ways — **Domestic (UAE)** vs **International** (defined as operations outside the UAE, including export sales) [FY2025 AR, Geographic segments, p.188]. Within the UAE, revenue is almost entirely **Dubai**: every named flagship community — Downtown Dubai, Dubai Creek Harbour, Dubai Hills, Emaar Beachfront, The Oasis — is in Dubai, and the results are datelined and framed around "Dubai's residential market" [Q4 FY2025 Press Release, 12-Feb-2026]. The filing does not give an emirate-level percentage, so the "Dubai" read is inference from the named assets, not a disclosed split.

| Geography | % of Revenue | Trend (Growing / Stable / Declining / Unknown) | Evidence | Risk |
|---|---:|---|---|---|
| **UAE** (Domestic — overwhelmingly Dubai) | **93%** (AED 46,153m) | **Growing** — 86% FY23 → 91% FY24 → 93% FY25 | [FY2025 AR, Geographic segments, p.188; FY23–24 from CIQ Financials→Segments (Geographic), reconciles to filing] | The entire business rides one city's property cycle. 97% of trade & unbilled receivables are from Middle East & North Africa operations [Note 34(a), p.213]. |
| **International** (Egypt — Emaar Misr; India — Emaar India; Turkey — Emaar Turkey; others) | **7%** (AED 3,404m) | **Declining share** — 14% FY23 → 9% FY24 → 7% FY25; roughly flat-to-down in absolute AED (3,725m → 3,311m → 3,404m) | [FY2025 AR, Geographic segments, p.188; CIQ Public Company Profile — subsidiaries] | Small and shrinking as UAE outgrows it; spread across several emerging markets. |

Shares sum to ~100% (UAE 93% + International 7%; there is no separate "Other"). The concentration is intensifying, not easing — UAE has risen ~7 points of revenue share in two years while International revenue is flat in absolute terms. The forward pipeline is similarly weighted: of a ~618m sq ft land bank, ~344m sq ft is in the UAE [Q4 FY2025 Press Release, 12-Feb-2026].

---

## 3. Concentration Flags

| Concentration Flag | Triggered (Y/N) | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| One customer >20% of revenue | **N** | Audited note: revenues come from "a large number of customers spread across different geographies"; no individual customer disclosed; customer default rate 0.5% of sales value [FY2025 AR, Note 34(a), p.213; AR p.23]. |
| Top 3 customers >40% of revenue | **N** | Same "large number of customers" disclosure; business is thousands of home-buyers plus 3,500+ retail tenants; no individual customer disclosed at any material share [FY2025 AR, Note 34(a), p.213; AR p.23]. |
| One geography >50% of revenue | **Y** | UAE = 93% of FY2025 revenue (AED 46,153m of AED 49,557m); 97% of trade & unbilled receivables from MENA [FY2025 AR, Geographic segments, p.188; Note 34(a), p.213]. |
| One customer or geography >30% with no long-term contract disclosed | **N** | UAE is >30% (93%), **but** a long-term contract structure IS disclosed: 95% of UAE revenue is recognised over time under instalment Sale & Purchase Agreements, and there is an AED 134.3bn UAE revenue backlog to be recognised over the next ~4 years [FY2025 AR, Geographic/Segment notes, p.188; AR p.23; Q4 FY2025 Press Release]. The near/medium-term concentration is contract-secured, not naked. The residual naked exposure is the **go-forward** dependence on new Dubai sales — a market/cycle risk, not a single-counterparty risk. |

---

## 4. Read

This is a **geography-concentrated** business, not a customer-concentrated one. On the customer side there is no concentration to speak of — the audited credit-risk note describes a large, granular buyer base (default rate just 0.5% of sales value), no customer clears the 20% or top-3 40% tests, and the CIQ "Customers" file is a related-party list, not a concentration. On the geography side the concentration is extreme and rising: the UAE — in practice Dubai — is 93% of revenue (up from 86% two years ago) and ~344m of ~618m sq ft of land bank. That concentration is **contractually secured in the near term, not naked**: 95% of UAE revenue is recognised over time under instalment sale contracts, backed by an AED 134.3bn UAE backlog (~AED 155bn group-wide, US$42.1bn) that converts to revenue over about four years. The single biggest dependency the synthesizer must carry forward is that **Emaar is a leveraged bet on the Dubai property cycle** — 93% of revenue and the majority of the land bank sit in one city, so a Dubai real-estate or regional-macro downturn hits almost the entire top line at once, with only the multi-year backlog as a buffer.

## business-model / 06_value-chain.md

_Source: `business-model/06_value-chain.md`_

# Value Chain Position — EMAR

*Emaar Properties PJSC (DFM: EMAAR) · Dubai/UAE master-planned real-estate developer · reports under IFRS in UAE dirham (AED), fiscal year ends 31 December. Upstream input: `02_business-identity.md`. Read alongside `10_external-dependency.md` — that agent owns the macro-cycle exposure; this report covers only the bargaining relationships with suppliers and customers.*

## 1. Stages Occupied

Emaar sits across five linked stages, from raw land to the end shopper. The dominant one by far is the developer engine (80% of revenue). *Off-plan = homes sold before they are built, paid in instalments during construction. Escrow = a regulated account (UAE RERA rules) that holds buyer cash and releases it to the developer as construction hits milestones. EBITDA = earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation — a rough cash-profit proxy.*

| Value Chain Stage | Company Role (1 sentence) | Bargaining Power vs Upstream | Bargaining Power vs Downstream | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Raw-material holder — land assembly & master-planning** | Holds and master-plans a ~600m sq ft land bank (UAE ~317–369m sq ft), most of it acquired historically at low cost, converting raw land into branded, serviced community plots. | **Mid** | **Strong** (transfer is internal, to its own development arm) | Land bank ~600m sq ft Q1 2026 / ~660m sq ft 3Q25 [Q1 2026 press release; Q3'25 earnings-call summary]; new land via 50-50 JV with a private landowner (Emaar Hills, AED 100bn, 40,000 units) and a 36m sq ft acquisition, AED 120bn gross development value *(total sales value the plots can eventually produce)* [Q4'25 & Q3'25 earnings-call summaries]; Government of Dubai via ICD 22.3%, "significant influence", is largest holder and city master-planner [FY2025 AR, related-party note; 10_external-dependency §1] |
| **Manufacturer / developer — build-to-sell, off-plan (dominant, 80% of revenue)** | Designs and sells homes off-plan before building them, then outsources the actual construction to third-party specialist contractors. | **Mid** | **Strong** | Real Estate AED 39,550m, 80% of AED 49,557m [ciq_facts.json segments_revenue; CIQ Financials → Segments 12M Dec-31-2025]; construction "handled by specialist contractors" [FY2025 AR, operations narrative — construction "handled by specialist contractors"]; named contractors Ahluwalia, Innovators Façade, Otis (elevators) [Suppliers.xls]; FY2025 launches hit 90–100% absorption "with no pressure on pricing" alongside raised prices [Q4'25 earnings-call summary] |
| **End-customer-facing brand / own sales channel** | Sells directly under the "Emaar" master-community brand (Downtown Dubai, Dubai Hills, Emaar Beachfront) to a fragmented base of ~80% first-time, largely foreign buyers, using external brokers only as paid agents. | n/a (internal) | **Strong** | 80% first-time buyers, top nationality India 20% [Q3'25 earnings-call summary]; ~4% average commission paid to external brokers — a cost-of-distribution, not a channel that controls the buyer [Q3'25 earnings-call summary] |
| **Landlord / retailer — malls & commercial leasing (15% of revenue)** | Owns and leases The Dubai Mall and ~1.4m sq m of retail/commercial space, charging base rent plus turnover rent *(extra rent tied to a tenant's own sales)* and service charges. | **Mid** | **Strong** | Leasing, Retail & Related AED 7,681m, 15% [ciq_facts.json segments_revenue]; mall occupancy ~98% at 31 Mar 2026 [Q1 2026 press release]; Dubai Mall 110m+ visitors in 2025 [Q4'25 earnings-call summary] |
| **Service provider — hospitality & leisure (5% of revenue)** | Owns and/or manages ~41 hotels (~10,000 keys) and paid attractions (Burj Khalifa observation decks, Dubai Fountain, Dubai Aquarium). | **Mid** | **Mid** | Hospitality AED 2,326m, 5% [ciq_facts.json segments_revenue]; UAE hotel occupancy ~82% FY2025 falling to 69% Q1 2026 — rates set by the Dubai tourism market, not by Emaar [Q4'25 & Q1 2026 press releases]; 75%+ of the hotel pipeline runs under management contracts [Q3'25 earnings-call summary] |

**Bargaining power bands:** Strong = Emaar sets price, dictates terms, has alternatives · Mid = negotiated, no extreme leverage either way · Weak = price-taker, terms imposed, few alternatives.

The pattern is consistent across every stage: Emaar is **Strong facing its customers** and **Mid facing its inputs**. It is nowhere a price-taker on its outputs; it is a partial price-taker only on commodity construction inputs and on incremental land.

## 2. Input Cost Pass-Through

Emaar has **no contractual mechanism to pass rising input costs back to buyers who have already bought.** Off-plan units are sold at a fixed price at launch, before construction, and the buyer pays fixed instalments during the ~4-year build; the pool discloses no cost-escalator or indexed-price clause in buyer contracts. So when steel, cement, labour and contractor prices rise during construction, Emaar absorbs the increase on the units already sold — the sold-but-not-yet-built backlog. That absorption is visible: gross margin *(sales minus the cost of the land and building in what was sold)* fell from 63% in FY2023 to 55% in FY2025, and management now guides "low 50s sustainably" over the medium term [ciq_facts.json margin_trend; Q4'25 earnings-call summary]. The offset — and it is a real one — is that Emaar re-prices at every **new** launch: it raised prices on FY2025 launches while still clearing 90–100% of units [Q4'25 earnings-call summary]. In plain terms, it cannot pass cost inflation *backward* into the ~AED 155bn signed backlog, but it does pass it *forward* into new launches, with a lag of one launch cycle. Construction cost itself runs through cost of sales of AED 22,330m on AED 49,557m revenue, ~45% [FY2025 AR, Industry-Specific tab, Total Cost of Sales AED 22,329.96m; ciq_facts.json segments].

**Supplier / input concentration (quantify).** The pool does **not** quantify supplier concentration — there is no disclosed share of cost of sales from the largest supplier or the top 3, and no single-source or sole-source component is flagged. *Not proven from available data* for a numeric input-concentration figure. What the pool does show is that construction is outsourced to a competitive, fragmented pool of specialist contractors (Ahluwalia Contracts, Innovators Façade, Otis for elevators, plus Indian-subsidiary-level contractors) with no one contractor sized as material [Suppliers.xls; FY2025 AR operations narrative]. Steel and cement are commodities bought largely *through* those contractors, so Emaar is a price-taker on the commodity but not dependent on any one vendor. The one genuinely concentrated, critical input is **land**, and the critical counterparty is the **Government of Dubai / Investment Corporation of Dubai (ICD)** — Emaar's 22.3% controlling shareholder with "significant influence," the city's master urban planner, and the source of incremental land (allocations and JVs such as the 50-50 Emaar Hills deal) [FY2025 AR related-party note; Q3'25 earnings-call summary]. A ~600m sq ft legacy land bank at low historical cost buffers this dependency for 10–15 years, but on *new* land Emaar takes the government's terms. This land + government node — not any raw material — is the material single-source-style dependency to carry into §5.

## 3. Customer Pricing Power

Emaar can raise prices without losing volume, and it has done so in the last 24 months. FY2025 launches "achieved 90–100% absorption rates alongside increased prices, reflecting strong demand with no pressure on pricing," and total property sales rose to a record AED 80bn, +15.6% YoY, with Q1 2026 up a further 16% to AED 22.4bn — price and volume rising together, the textbook signature of pricing power [Q4'25 & Q1 2026 earnings-call summaries / press releases]. The customer base carries no concentration risk: buyers are individual retail and high-net-worth investors, ~80% of them first-time buyers, the largest single nationality only ~20% (India) — so no buyer can dictate terms [Q3'25 earnings-call summary; Customers.xls shows no material single external customer]. Emaar's leverage over the buyer is unusually hard: buyers **forward-fund** the build through instalments into regulated escrow (~AED 44bn held), so customers pay before they receive the finished home — the customer finances Emaar's working capital, not the other way round [Q3'25 earnings-call summary]. On the mall side the same holds — ~98% occupancy and 110m+ annual visitors give Emaar the whip hand over retail tenants [Q1 2026 & Q4'25]. The one caveat is that this pricing power is **cyclical, not structural**: it rides a record Dubai up-cycle, and consensus long-term growth of −14.8% signals the market expects the cycle to roll over, at which point absorption and pricing weaken regardless of brand (base rate: the 2015–2019 and 2009 Dubai downturns) [ciq_facts.json consensus_view; 10_external-dependency §3].

## 4. Economic Control Verdict

**Mixed.**

Emaar is dominant over its customers and only a partial price-taker on its inputs — strong on one side, weaker on the other. Downstream it sets price and payment terms, raised prices into 90–100% absorption, faces a fragmented buyer base with no concentration, and is forward-funded by buyer cash in escrow — this is close to full control of its own output economics [Q4'25 earnings-call summary; Q3'25 escrow AED 44bn]. It is held out of a clean "Controls economics" verdict by two upstream facts: it absorbs commodity and labour cost inflation on its fixed-price sold backlog with no pass-through clause (gross margin 63% → 55%, guided low-50s), and its single most critical input — land, plus the visa/population and tax policy that manufactures demand — is set by the Government of Dubai / ICD, its own 22.3% controller, not by Emaar (the new 15% top-up tax alone added AED 2,114m of tax in 2025, imposed by the state) [ciq_facts.json margin_trend; FY2025 AR tax note; 10_external-dependency §1]. It is nowhere near "Squeezed": a competitive contractor pool, a huge low-cost land buffer, and ~AED 25bn net cash *(cash above all debt, CIQ broad basis)* mean no supplier can corner it either [ciq_facts.json net_debt/total_debt].

## 5. The Single Biggest Bargaining Risk

The **Government of Dubai / ICD upstream relationship** — the counterparty that simultaneously supplies Emaar's scarcest input (land + master-plan approvals) and sets the visa, population and tax policy that creates its buyer demand, while holding 22.3% control — is the one value-chain link where Emaar takes terms rather than sets them, and its deterioration (tighter land allocation, adverse policy, or further tax) would hurt most.

## business-model / 07_business-quality.md

_Source: `business-model/07_business-quality.md`_

# Business Quality — EMAR

*Emaar Properties PJSC (DFM: EMAAR). Dubai (UAE) master-planned real-estate developer. IFRS, reporting currency AED (dirham, pegged to the US dollar at ~3.6725). All figures FY2025 (year ended 31 Dec 2025) or LTM to 31 Mar 2026 unless stated. Upstream inputs present: `02_business-identity`, `03_segment-map`, `05_customer-geography` — no degraded-confidence note needed.*

**Sector overlay (step 2b).** Business type from `02_business-identity` = **REIT / real estate** (with the caveat that Emaar is predominantly a *build-to-sell developer*, not a rent-collecting REIT — ~80% of revenue is one-time off-plan unit sales, ~20% is recurring mall/hotel income). **Sector overlay applied: REIT / real estate — factors capital intensity, margin stability, cyclicality, and repeat/recurring revenue use the sector-specific lens** (capital intensity read as LTV / asset-heaviness rather than plant capex; cyclicality read as *Dubai property-cycle severity*; margin stability read as same-store recurring-NOI stability plus developer-mix swing; recurring revenue read as lease visibility plus the contracted pre-sales backlog). The other seven factors use the generic lens.

## 1. Quality Factor Table

| Quality Factor | Score /100 | Evidence | Comment |
|---|---:|---|---|
| Pricing power *(higher = better)* | 62 | 48 FY2025 launches at "90–100% absorption rates alongside increased prices... no pressure on pricing"; management guides gross margin "low 50s sustainably over the medium term" [Q4 2025 earnings call summary, 16 Feb 2026]. Brand premium from Downtown Dubai / Burj Khalifa halo [FY2025 Annual Report — Principal Activities]. | Genuine premium-brand pricing power, but read it at a cycle peak: in the 2015–2020 Dubai downturn developers cut prices and stacked incentives. Real, brand-backed, but cycle-conditioned — not staple-grade durable. |

Only 20% of sales from repeat buyers; 80% first-time [Q3 2025 earnings call summary, 10 Nov 2025]. AED 155bn contracted backlog gives ~4-year revenue *visibility* [Q4 2025 earnings call summary]. | Structurally ~80% is transactional one-off home sales, not recurring. The recurring annuity is only a fifth; the pre-sold backlog buys visibility, not renewal. Middle-band. |

Malls ~98% occupancy = sticky tenants [Q1 2026 press release]. Tenants stickier. Nets to average. |

Recurring leasing segment stable at ~69% margin [FY2025 AR, Note 3, p.188]. | The stable ~69% mall annuity is real but small; the dominant developer margin swings ~20 points on mix and on the legacy-cheap-land-vs-selling-price spread, which narrows as new land is bought at market prices. Below average. |

Off-plan model self-funds construction via buyer instalments (AED 44bn in project escrow) [Q3 2025 earnings call summary]; Real Estate segment fixed capex only 0.8% of segment revenue [FY2025 AR, Note 3, p.188]; fixed-asset turnover 5.3x [CIQ→Ratios, LTM]. | On the REIT lens (LTV = capital risk), LTV is essentially negative — a clear strength. Tempered by an asset-heavy ~600m sq ft land bank and a planned AED 65bn capex over 5 years [Q4 2025 earnings call summary] — but that capex is funded from operating cash, not debt. |

Mixed. |

No technology substitution threatens the core develop-and-sell model. *(Inference, not from filings.)* | The threat to Emaar is the *cycle*, not disruption. Rate-of-change is low → high score. Input exposure is construction cost (steel/cement/labour). ROIC swung 4.7% (2021) → 13.7% (LTM) [CIQ→Ratios]. Consensus long-term growth **−14.8%** [`ciq_facts.json` consensus_view]. 93% single-city Dubai concentration [FY2025 AR, geographic segments, p.188]. | Dubai property is among the most cyclical real-estate markets globally (~50% peak-to-trough in 2008–09; ~35% in 2015–20). One city, one asset class, at a cycle high. The AED 155bn backlog cushions ~4 years of revenue and net cash ensures survival — hence not lower — but this is the factor that defines the business. Weakest factor. |
| Disclosure quality *(higher = better)* | 68 | Three consistent IFRS 8 segments with segment-level profit, capex, assets and geography [FY2025 AR, Note 3, p.187–188]; developer KPIs disclosed — pre-sales, AED 155bn backlog, land bank, units, occupancy [Q4 2025 / Q1 2026 press releases]; rated S&P BBB+ / Moody's Baa1 stable [Q4 2025 press release]. Gaps: no cap rate, no WALE (lease length), no group average selling price, no FFO/AFFO [`02_business-identity` KPI checklist]. | Good, granular financial disclosure; the missing metrics are real-estate-specific valuation inputs, not opacity. Arabic-original filing is not a data gap (§27). Strong. |

Bands (per `CLAUDE.md`): 0–20 very weak · 21–40 weak · 41–60 mixed/average · 61–80 strong · 81–100 very strong.

## 2. Aggregate Quality Score

**Aggregate business quality: 53 / 100 (Mixed / Average).**

This is a judgment-weighted aggregate, not a straight average (the simple mean of the 11 rows is ~55). **Cyclicality carries the heaviest weight (~30%)** because it defines what Emaar is — a leveraged bet on one city's property cycle, currently at a peak — and it drags hardest (27). **Margin stability and competitive intensity are the secondary drags (~20% combined).** Against them, a quality floor of ~50% weight — pricing power (62), low disruption risk (72), net-cash-driven capital intensity (64), commodity independence (62), and good disclosure (68) — keeps the score out of the Weak band. **Band anchor (fix F43):** the second-lowest row is margin stability at 44, so the aggregate is capped at ~64; 53 sits comfortably below that ceiling and above the 27 cyclicality floor, reconstructable from the rows.

## 3. Strongest Factor & Weakest Factor

| | Factor | Score | Why |
|---|---|---:|---|
| Strongest | Industry rate-of-change / disruption risk | 72 | Real-estate development is a slow-changing, established industry; Emaar is the sorted incumbent (>129,100 units delivered since 2002), and no technology shift threatens the develop-and-sell model. The business's risk is the property cycle, not obsolescence. |
| Weakest | Cyclicality | 27 | 93% of revenue rides the Dubai property cycle — one of the world's most cyclical (revenue −10.6% in FY2022, writedowns FY2021–23, hospitality loss in FY2020, ROIC swinging 4.7%→13.7%). Consensus already models −14.8% long-term growth off the current peak. |

## 4. Read

Emaar is a **high-quality but deeply cyclical single-city real-estate developer at a cyclical peak**, wrapped around a smaller recurring mall-and-hotel annuity (~20% of revenue) that carries the quality and cushions the downside. The assets, the Downtown-Dubai brand, the net-cash balance sheet (Total Debt/EBITDA 0.40x), and the capital-light off-plan model (buyers pre-fund construction through escrow) are all genuine strengths — but they sit on top of one city's property cycle, so the business classifies as **cyclical, not durable compounder.** Crucially, this is a **sector/property-cycle bet, not a technology-disruption bet**: the industry rate-of-change row scored 72 (well above 40), so §24 Filter 5 does **not** trip — the danger is the cycle turning, not the model being disrupted, and RF-BQ-005 is **not** emitted.

The headline returns are at a cyclical high and must be anchored, not extrapolated: **LTM ROIC of 13.7% (the profit earned on each AED 100 of capital) is a peak** — the FY2021–FY2025 span ran 4.7% → 5.7% → 8.5% → 9.8% → 12.5%, so a **through-cycle ROIC is nearer high-single-digits (~8–10%)**, and today's ~55% gross margin / ~49% EBITDA margin are similarly flattered by the wide spread between historically cheap legacy land and current selling prices — a spread that narrows as Emaar buys new land at market prices (AED 120bn gross development value acquired in 2025). The strong current pricing power (row 62) does **not** override the low cyclicality row (27); the two reconcile as "premium pricing power *while the Dubai cycle is up*."

**The single factor a buyer should watch over the next 24 months: Dubai pre-sales momentum and the developer margin.** New bookings (property sales, AED 80bn in FY2025) are the true leading indicator — they turn *before* IFRS revenue, which the AED 155bn backlog carries for ~4 years. If Dubai sales cool, bookings and margin roll first while reported revenue stays elevated on the backlog; that gap is where the peak-cycle risk shows up.

## business-model / 08_competitive-map.md

_Source: `business-model/08_competitive-map.md`_

# Competitive Map — EMAR

*Emaar Properties PJSC (DFM:EMAAR). UAE / Dubai issuer, IFRS, reporting currency AED; the dirham is pegged to the US dollar at ~3.67 AED/USD. Both required upstreams are present — `02_business-identity.md` and `03_segment-map.md` — and are inherited below. Peer economics are captured for the downstream `moat` agent's "earns more than peers" check; peer margins that are not publicly disclosed are marked as such and never invented.*

## 1. Dominant Segment

**Real Estate — the build-and-sell (off-plan) developer engine: 79.8% of FY2025 revenue and 74.9% of segment profit, concentrated in Dubai residential** [inherited from `03_segment-map.md`; FY2025 Annual Report (IFRS), Note 3, p.187–188]. "Off-plan" means homes sold before/during construction and paid in instalments. Competitors below are chosen for this segment — Dubai (and wider UAE) residential development — not for the smaller mall-and-hotel annuity.

## 2. Named Competitors

Three most-credible rivals in the dominant segment: the two largest direct Dubai off-plan developers after Emaar (DAMAC, Sobha), plus the one listed UAE developer peer that carries disclosed economics (Aldar) so the moat has a clean peer-margin anchor.

### Competitor A — DAMAC Properties

- **Ticker / listing:** Private since 2022 (formerly DFM:DAMAC; taken private by founder Hussain Sajwani's Maple Invest for ~AED 2.19bn) [Web: DAMAC Properties / Wikipedia, 2026 — unverified]. Its DIFC debt issuer, Damac Real Estate Development Ltd, is rated by S&P.
- **Where they compete:** Dubai off-plan residential — ultra-luxury branded residences (Versace, Cavalli tie-ups); same forward-funded, instalment-sale model as Emaar; expanding into Iraq/Saudi/international.
- **Scale:** AED 36bn property sales in 2025 (a record; the largest of Dubai's *private* developers, ~45% of Emaar's AED 80.4bn) [Web: Gulf News, 9-Feb-2026; Time Homes Real Estate ranking, 2026 — unverified]. 2024 revenue is reported inconsistently across web sources (~AED 13.1bn vs ~AED 18.7bn); the higher figure is paired with ~AED 4.8bn net profit [Web: apilproperties / Owler, 2026 — unverified].
- **Profitability / return on capital:** Not publicly disclosed in audited detail (private). Web-reported ~AED 4.8bn net profit on ~AED 18.7bn 2024 revenue implies a ~26% net margin — **unverified**, figures conflict, treat as directional only [Web, 2026 — unverified]. For the moat: DAMAC is a partial anchor at best; ROIC/ROE not disclosed.
- **Source named in:** Industry press consistently ranks DAMAC the clear #2 Dubai developer behind Emaar [Web: Gulf News; Time Homes; Oliva "Emaar vs DAMAC", 2026]. Not named in Emaar's own filings; not in the CIQ comp set (private).
- **One-line read:** The direct #2 in Dubai by sales — branded-luxury off-plan, roughly half Emaar's booking volume, and the sharpest private rival for the same buyer.

### Competitor B — Sobha Realty

- **Ticker / listing:** Private (UAE operating arm of the Sobha group; holding company PNC Investments rated Moody's Ba3→upgraded Ba2, with a USD 500m sukuk — Islamic bond) [Web: Moody's via Sobha Realty press, 2024–2025 — unverified]. Not the separately-listed Indian Sobha Ltd (BOM:532784).
- **Where they compete:** Dubai off-plan residential — vertically-integrated luxury communities (Sobha Hartland, Siniya Island); 11 UAE masterplans; same off-plan instalment model.
- **Scale:** AED 23bn sales in 2024 (+~50% YoY); ~AED 30bn in 2025 on stated targets (AED 20bn Dubai + AED 10bn Siniya Island) [Web: Sobha Realty press; Construction Week, 2024–2026 — unverified].
- **Profitability / return on capital:** Not publicly disclosed (private); revenue and net margin not broken out. Only the sukuk rating (speculative-grade Ba2) and sales are public. ROIC/ROE **not disclosed** — not a usable peer margin anchor.
- **Source named in:** Industry press ranks Sobha the #3 Dubai developer and puts its 2024 share at "~10% of Dubai's real estate market" [Web: Sobha Realty press; royalpproperties / miva rankings, 2025–2026 — unverified]. Not named in Emaar's filings; not in the CIQ comp set.
- **One-line read:** A pure Dubai off-plan luxury rival at ~10% share — smaller than DAMAC by sales, but the same buyer and the same forward-funded model.

### Competitor C — Aldar Properties PJSC

- **Ticker / listing:** ADX:ALDAR (Abu Dhabi Securities Exchange) — the largest listed UAE developer, so the only rival here with audited, comparable economics.
- **Where they compete:** UAE residential development, historically Abu Dhabi-centric, now expanding into Dubai; a larger recurring / asset-management and construction mix alongside build-to-sell.
- **Scale:** FY2025 revenue AED 33.8bn (+47% YoY); group sales/bookings AED 40.6bn (+21%), of which UAE AED 35.5bn [Web: Aldar FY2025 results via Zawya / The National / Khaleej Times, 9-Feb-2026]. About two-thirds of Emaar's AED 49.6bn revenue and roughly half Emaar's AED 80.4bn bookings.
- **Profitability / return on capital:** FY2025 EBITDA AED 11.2bn (~33% margin — cash-profit before interest, tax, depreciation) and net profit after tax AED 8.8bn (+36%), a ~26% net margin [Web: Aldar FY2025 results, 9-Feb-2026]. CIQ comp cross-check (LTM): gross 34.9%, EBITDA 28.9%, **operating (EBIT) margin 27.2%, net income margin 23.0%** [CIQ "Company Comparable Analysis" → Operating Statistics, as-of 2026-06-28]. **ROE/ROIC not disclosed in available sources** (not carried in the CIQ comp export; no clean equity figure sourced) — the profit-margin anchor stands in for it. **Peer anchor for the moat:** Aldar earns an operating margin of ~27% and net margin of ~23–26%, versus Emaar's ~45% EBIT / ~36% net margin and ~13% ROIC — Emaar out-earns its one listed peer by a wide gap [Emaar: CIQ Operating Statistics; ciq_facts.json `multi_year_trajectory` ROIC 12.5% FY2025 → 13.7% LTM].
- **Source named in:** In the pool CIQ comp set (the sole other UAE developer among 11 names) and named in Emaar's own FY2025 Annual Report — as a co-participant in the "Unity for Change" retail-sustainability initiative and as counterparty to a Dubai Holding–Aldar mixed-use JV [FY2025 Annual Report, ESG / Board sections; CIQ "Company Comparable Analysis" → Business Description].
- **One-line read:** The listed UAE peer and the moat's clean margin benchmark — comparable revenue scale, but development-plus-asset-management economics that run at roughly half Emaar's operating margin.

## 3. Competitive Position

**Holding — Emaar is the clear #1 in Dubai residential development and stays there by a wide margin, though fast-growing private rivals keep the gap from widening.** Developer-level market share is not officially published, so booking (property-sales) value is the proxy: Emaar sold AED 80.4bn in FY2025 (+16% YoY), roughly double #2 DAMAC's AED 36bn; over Jan–Aug 2025 Emaar's ~AED 51bn was again ~2x DAMAC's ~AED 24bn [Q4 2025 press release, 12-Feb-2026; Web: Time Homes / Gulf News rankings, 2026 — unverified]. Supporting proxies point the same way: a revenue backlog (sold, not yet recognised) of AED 163.4bn at 31-Mar-2026 and 90–100% absorption on FY2025 launches [Q1 2026 press release; Q4 2025 earnings call summary]. The reason this is "holding" and not clearly "gaining": DAMAC (record AED 36bn) and Sobha (+~50% in 2024) grew faster in percentage terms off smaller bases, so Emaar's ~2x lead is stable rather than expanding.

## 4. Competitive Shape

**Consolidated-but-competitive, led by one dominant player — a "leader-plus-cluster" oligopoly of branded developers sitting above a state-owned master-developer bloc.** A handful of large names supply most new Dubai off-plan stock: by 2025 sales value, Emaar AED 80.4bn, DAMAC ~36, Sobha ~30, Binghatti ~26, with state-owned Nakheel (~AED 13bn Jan–Aug) and Meraas (~AED 10bn Jan–Aug) — both now consolidated under Dubai Holding Real Estate — behind them [Q4 2025 press release; Web: Time Homes / royalpproperties rankings, 2025–2026 — unverified]. Sobha alone put its 2024 share at ~10%, which frames the order of magnitude: no single firm monopolises, but the top ~6 branded developers dominate new supply. A formal concentration index (HHI) and official per-developer shares are not published — the Dubai total of 270,000+ transactions worth AED 892bn in 2025 mixes resale and all segments, a different base from developer primary sales, so it is not a clean share denominator [Q4 2025 earnings call summary]. One structural twist: the state-owned bloc is both rival and partner — Emaar's UAE Development and Rove Hotels run as joint ventures with Meraas (co-opetition) [FY2025 Annual Report, Note / segment and hospitality sections].

## 5. Caveat

Two limits on this map, both disclosed rather than papered over:
1. **Emaar's own filings do not name competitors in a rivalry sense.** Aldar, Meraas and Nakheel appear only as JV partners, an ESG co-participant, or in director biographies — not in a "our competitors are…" disclosure. Competitor identification therefore leans on the in-pool CIQ comp set (Aldar) plus industry press (DAMAC, Sobha, Binghatti).
2. **The two largest *direct* Dubai rivals (DAMAC, Sobha) are private, so their margins and returns are not audited-public.** DAMAC's revenue/profit figures conflict across web sources and are unverified; Sobha discloses only sales and a sukuk rating. Only Aldar carries a clean, sourced peer margin — so the moat's per-peer profitability comparison rests mainly on Aldar, with DAMAC/Sobha as directional at best. **What would resolve it:** DAMAC's DIFC sukuk-issuer accounts (Damac Real Estate Development Ltd) and Sobha/PNC Investments sukuk disclosures for audited peer margins and returns; Dubai Land Department developer-level sales data for hard market shares.

## business-model / 09_moat.md

_Source: `business-model/09_moat.md`_

# Moat — EMAR

*Emaar Properties PJSC (DFM: EMAAR). Dubai/UAE master-planned real-estate developer; IFRS, reporting currency AED (dirham pegged to the US dollar at ~3.6725 AED/USD). Upstream `08_competitive-map.md` is present — no degraded-confidence note needed. Named competitors are inherited from it; no new competitors are introduced. Business type = operating company (property developer), so the economic test uses **ROIC vs WACC**, not ROE/cost-of-equity. "Off-plan" = homes sold before they are built and paid for in instalments during construction.*

## 1. Named Competitors

- **DAMAC Properties** — the direct #2 in Dubai off-plan by sales (~AED 36bn property sales in 2025, ~45% of Emaar's AED 80.4bn); private since 2022, so margins/returns are not audited-public. [`08_competitive-map.md` §2A]
- **Sobha Realty** — pure Dubai off-plan luxury rival at ~10% market share (~AED 30bn 2025 sales); private (Sobha group / PNC Investments), only a sukuk rating and sales disclosed. [`08_competitive-map.md` §2B]
- **Aldar Properties PJSC (ADX: ALDAR)** — the largest *listed* UAE developer and the only rival with clean audited economics; comparable revenue scale (FY2025 AED 33.8bn) but development-plus-asset-management economics at roughly half Emaar's operating margin. The moat's clean peer-margin benchmark. [`08_competitive-map.md` §2C]

## 2. Moat Sources

Strength bands (CLAUDE.md §12): 0–20 very weak · 21–40 weak · 41–60 mixed · 61–80 strong · 81–100 very strong.

| Possible Moat | Present? (Y/N) | Evidence | Strength /100 |
|---|---|---|---:|
| Brand | **Y** | The "Emaar" master-community brand built on iconic destinations — Downtown Dubai, Burj Khalifa, The Dubai Mall, Dubai Hills, Emaar Beachfront — commands a demonstrated price premium: FY2025's 48 launches hit "90–100% absorption alongside increased prices… no pressure on pricing." Genuine, but the premium is cycle-conditioned (developers cut prices in the 2015–2020 Dubai downturn), so not staple-grade. [`02_business-identity.md` §1; Q4 2025 earnings call summary, 16 Feb 2026; `07_business-quality.md` pricing-power row] | 68 |
| Cost advantage | **Y** | Two real edges: (1) a legacy land bank carried at ~AED 81/sq ft historical cost against today's selling prices — the spread that drives a 55% gross margin vs Aldar's ~35%; (2) the capital-light off-plan model — buyers forward-fund construction (advances AED 40.7bn, ~AED 44bn in regulated escrow), so the developer runs on negative working capital. But the land-spread half is **narrowing**: gross margin fell 63% (FY2023) → 55% (FY2025), guided "low 50s," as new land is bought at market prices (36m sq ft, AED 120bn gross development value, in 2025). [`04_unit-economics.md` §2; `06_value-chain.md` §2; ciq_facts.json margin_trend] | 60 |
| Distribution | **N** | Sells direct under its own master-brand but uses external brokers only as paid agents (~4% commission) — a cost of distribution, not a channel Emaar controls; the value-chain read is explicit that brokers "do not control the buyer." No distribution lock-in. [`06_value-chain.md` §1, §3] | 30 |
| Scale | **Y** | Clear #1 in Dubai residential: AED 80.4bn property sales in FY2025, ~2x #2 DAMAC's AED 36bn; >129,100 units delivered since 2002; AED 163.4bn revenue backlog; ~600m sq ft land bank. Scale gives contractor/purchasing leverage and brand amortisation — but Aldar has comparable *revenue* scale at half the margin, so scale alone is not what drives Emaar's premium. [`08_competitive-map.md` §3; `02_business-identity.md` §3a] | 55 |
| Technology / IP | **N** | No meaningful technology or intellectual-property moat in master-planned development; construction is outsourced to a fragmented contractor pool. Industry rate-of-change is low (business-quality 72/100) — the threat is the cycle, not disruption — so the *absence* of a tech moat is not itself a risk. [`07_business-quality.md` rate-of-change row; `06_value-chain.md` §2] | 15 |
| Licenses / regulation | **Y (double-edged)** | Privileged historical access to prime Dubai land via the Government of Dubai / Investment Corporation of Dubai (ICD), the ~22.3% controlling shareholder and city master-planner — that first-mover allocation gave Emaar Downtown Dubai. But this is a *dependency* Emaar does not control (external-dependency ranks it the #1 bargaining risk), RERA escrow rules apply to all developers equally, and new land now comes at market via JV/allocation. More relationship than defensible moat. [`06_value-chain.md` §2, §5; `10_external-dependency.md` §1 (Government policy row)] | 42 |
| Network effects | **N** | No true network effect in home-selling. There is a mild integrated-destination flywheel — Dubai Mall footfall (110m+ visitors) lifts Downtown residential values — but that is a brand/location synergy, not a user-network effect. [`06_value-chain.md` §1 (leasing row); `02_business-identity.md` §1] | 25 |
| Switching costs | **N** | High *in-contract* lock-in (0.5% buyer default rate, forfeiture on exit, title passes only on final payment) — but that is contractual, not a switching-cost moat. Post-handover there is near-zero stickiness: ~80% first-time buyers, no ongoing relationship. Mall tenants are stickier (~98% occupancy) but that is the small 15% leasing segment. [`07_business-quality.md` customer-stickiness row; `06_value-chain.md` §3] | 30 |
| Natural resource access | **Y** | A ~600m sq ft land bank (UAE ~317m) in prime, finite Dubai locations, most acquired historically at low cost — a genuine scarce-resource advantage that buffers ~10–15 years. Overlaps the cost-advantage row; incremental land now comes at market prices, so the *cheap* portion is fixed and dilutes over time. [`06_value-chain.md` §1–2; `04_unit-economics.md` §2] | 60 |
| Location advantage | **Y** | Downtown Dubai (Burj Khalifa, The Dubai Mall, Dubai Fountain) is an irreplaceable location that cannot be rebuilt by a rival — the single most valuable destination cluster in Dubai, owned and controlled by Emaar, and the anchor of the residential price premium. The most durable single pillar. [`02_business-identity.md` §1; `06_value-chain.md` §1] | 65 |

**The moat is real but narrow and integrated:** brand (68), location (65), low-cost land / natural-resource access (60) are one linked advantage — the dominant Dubai brand is *built on* irreplaceable Downtown-Dubai land bought cheaply. This is why Emaar out-earns every named peer on margin. Distribution, technology, network effects and switching costs are not moats here.

| Competitor 3 — Aldar | 34.9% | 27.2% | Not disclosed (ROE/ROIC not in CIQ export; net margin 23.0% stands in) | LTM (as-of 2026-06-28) | `08_competitive-map.md` §2C, citing CIQ Company Comparable Analysis → Operating Statistics |

*Per-peer figures are taken from `competitive-map`'s profiles (captured upstream); only DAMAC/Sobha are re-checked and remain "not disclosed" — private, so no audited margin exists. Not invented.*

**Return-metric note (management-headline cross-check).** The 12.5%/13.7% ROIC is a Capital-IQ vendor computation, not a management headline; it reconciles with the business-quality through-cycle read (FY2021→LTM: 4.7% → 5.7% → 8.5% → 9.8% → 12.5% → 13.7%). The ~45% EBIT margin is CIQ Operating Statistics; note Emaar's reported profit before tax (AED 25,656m, ~52% of revenue) runs *above* EBIT because of large non-operating finance income (on the ~AED 35bn cash and on instalment receivables) and JV share — so the operating EBIT margin, not the PBT margin, is the correct moat input. [`10_external-dependency.md` §1 (PBT AED 25,656m); `04_unit-economics.md`]

**NOPAT tax normalization (anchor for the DCF).** NOPAT = EBIT × (1 − tax rate). The normalized **structural tax rate used here is 15%** — the UAE Domestic Minimum Top-up Tax (the OECD "Pillar Two" jurisdictional minimum), now the forward rate. What is stripped: FY2025's *reported* ~13% effective rate was cushioned by a one-off relief, and — the larger distortion — **FY2021–FY2023 carried near-zero corporate tax** (UAE had no corporate income tax before FY2024), so the CIQ ROIC series is *tax-flattered in its early years*. Normalizing the whole series to 15% trims the LTM peak from 13.7% to **~13.4%** and the raw through-cycle average from ~8.2% to **~7.5%** (ex-COVID-trough FY2023–25 normalized ≈ 9.5%). This 15% rate is the anchor `valuation/04_intrinsic-dcf` (§1) must reconcile its NOPAT to — the moat ROIC and the DCF must not diverge on the tax rate.

**Net-cash / gross-capital check.** Emaar holds ~AED 25bn net cash / ~AED 35bn gross cash (total debt AED 10.1bn − net debt −AED 25.0bn = AED 35.0bn cash). The classic net-cash distortion — where netting cash *out* of the capital base collapses the denominator and inflates ROIC — **does not bite here**: CIQ computes ROIC on total capital (debt + equity) *without* netting cash, so the large cash pile sits *inside* the base and if anything **dilutes** the reported ROIC. The 13.7%/12.5% headline is therefore the conservative (cash-in-base, gross-capital) read; an operating ROIC that stripped the idle cash would be *higher*, not lower. Either way the conclusion holds: through the cycle, after 15% tax, the return is ~7.5–9.5%. *(Convention note: Inference on CIQ's invested-capital definition, not from filings.)*

**The economic moat test (required).**

> Return on capital **at / below** cost of capital through the cycle: **~7.5–9.5% through-cycle ROIC** (15%-tax-normalized; 13.4% LTM *peak*) vs **~11–12% WACC** — a gap of roughly **−200 to −450 bps through the cycle**; the return clears the WACC by only ~+150–220 bps *at the cyclical peak* and shrinks to roughly parity once tax-normalized. [WACC basis: CAPM estimate = risk-free ~4.5% (US 10Y, AED pegged to USD) + beta ~1.15 × UAE equity-risk-premium ~6.0% ≈ **~11.4%**; net-cash balance sheet means WACC ≈ cost of equity; plausible range ~10–12.5%. **Inference, not from filings** (CLAUDE.md §3) — no company-disclosed hurdle rate, WACC or cost of equity in the pool.]

The verdict is robust across the WACC range: even at the low end (~10%), the tax-normalized through-cycle ~7.5–9.5% sits at or below cost of capital, and only the *peak* year clears it.

## 4. Where The Company Sits

1. **Relative to peers:** **Company sits at the top of named peers on margin and (where disclosed) capital efficiency** — 55% gross / ~45% EBIT vs Aldar's 34.9% / 27.2% (an ~18-point EBIT gap), and ~2x #2 DAMAC's sales; DAMAC/Sobha margins are undisclosed (private) but Emaar's sales lead and premium positioning place it top-of-set. The peer-superiority is real and wide.
2. **Absolute (the economic moat test):** **The company earns a return on capital *above* its cost of capital only at the cyclical peak (13.4% normalized vs ~11.4% WACC) and *at or below* it through the cycle (~7.5–9.5% vs ~11.4%).** This is the decisive test — and it shows the wide peer-margin lead does **not** reliably convert into economic value-creation once the Dubai cycle and the new 15% tax are through-cycled.

## 5. Moat Verdict

**Narrow moat.**

The strongest moat is the **Emaar brand (68/100), inseparable from the irreplaceable Downtown-Dubai location (65) and the low-cost legacy land bank (60)** — one integrated advantage that lets Emaar out-earn its one audited peer (Aldar) by ~18 EBIT-margin points and hold ~2x the #2's sales. That advantage is genuine and evidenced. But it is capped at Narrow by the economic test: through the Dubai cycle, and after the new 15% structural tax, the return on capital is only **~7.5–9.5%** against a **~11–12% cost of capital** — it clears the hurdle only at the cyclical peak. **Hard rule applied (CLAUDE.md / module §3): because through-cycle ROIC sits at or below WACC, the verdict cannot be "Strong moat" despite the wide peer-margin superiority — this is closer to a moat in *structure* (brand, location, scale) than in *economics* through the cycle, and Narrow is the ceiling.** The durability test it must pass over the next 5 years: hold pricing and absorption as ~167,000 new Dubai units complete into 2026–27 (consensus already models −14.8% long-term growth), and defend the margin as the cheap-legacy-land spread narrows toward market-priced new land. Industry rate-of-change is low (business-quality 72/100), so §24 Filter 5 does **not** trip and durability is *not* discounted for disruption — the risk is the property cycle, not obsolescence.

**Moat trajectory — eroding.** Separate from the *level* (Narrow), the *direction* of the **economic** moat is eroding, even though headline returns sit at a cyclical peak: (1) the cost-advantage spread is structurally narrowing — gross margin 63% (FY2023) → 55% (FY2025), guided "low 50s," as new land is bought at market (AED 120bn GDV in 2025); (2) the new 15% DMTT tax permanently lowers after-tax returns versus the pre-2024 zero-tax regime the historical ROIC was earned under; (3) competitive intensity is rising at the peak (DAMAC record AED 36bn, Sobha +~50%, plus Binghatti/Danube); (4) consensus prices a −14.8% long-term contraction, i.e. the return-vs-WACC gap is cyclically elevated now and expected to compress. The one *stable* pillar is the brand + Downtown-Dubai location, which is not disappearing. Net: the economic advantage (return above cost of capital) is eroding behind a peak-cycle headline — the early-warning signal for the peak-return / declining-perpetuity treatment in `valuation/04` (§5) and `valuation/07`; peak-year returns must be anchored, not extrapolated.

## business-model / 10_external-dependency.md

_Source: `business-model/10_external-dependency.md`_

# External Dependency Check — EMAAR

*Emaar Properties PJSC (DFM: EMAAR) — Dubai / UAE real-estate developer. Reporting standard IFRS, currency AED (pegged to USD at ~3.6725), fiscal year = calendar year. All figures FY2025 (year ended 31 Dec 2025) unless stated [FY2025 Integrated Annual Report; 00_data-triage §2A].*

**The split that matters.** Emaar's own balance-sheet market risks — interest rates and FX on its debt and cash — are genuinely small: the dirham is pegged to the US dollar, total debt is AED 9.8bn against cash and short-term deposits of AED 71.5bn (net cash AED 61.7bn on a **broad basis** that nets in short-term deposits — the company's own footnote; see §15 hygiene note below) [FY2025 Annual Report, Financial Review — Net Cash, p.13]. But that is not what drives the equity. About 80% of revenue is off-plan Dubai residential development — homes sold to buyers before they are finished — funded by a heavily foreign buyer base. The outcome is set by the Dubai property cycle, foreign-capital inflows, government population/visa/ownership policy, regional geopolitics, and now a new UAE tax regime. Management controls pricing, launch timing, product mix and cash discipline *within* that cycle; it does not set the cycle.

## 1. Dependency Table

| External Variable | Dependency Level (Low / Mid / High) | Why It Matters | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| Commodity prices (construction materials, contractor labour) | Mid | Construction inputs sit inside cost of sales — housing cost of sales runs at roughly 45% of Real Estate segment revenue [segment-map §1; FY2025 Annual Report, Note 3]. Input-cost inflation compresses the spread between land cost and selling price, even though the company says pricing and mix offset it: "Despite higher activity levels and inflationary pressures, margins remained resilient, underpinned by strong pricing, a favourable product mix and ongoing cost-efficiency initiatives" [FY2025 Annual Report, Financial Review, p.13]. No sensitivity table is disclosed for a given percentage move in build cost — this is a qualitative flag, not a quantified one. |
| Interest rates | Mid | Own balance sheet: near-immaterial. A ±100 basis-point move (0.01 percentage points is one basis point) changes profit before tax by only AED 26.2m (2025) / AED 29.9m (2024) against PBT of AED 25,656m — about 0.1% [FY2025 Annual Report, Note 34(b) — Market risk, p.215]. Only ~AED 635m of debt is floating-rate (3-month EIBOR + 0.9%) out of AED 9.8bn total debt [CIQ Financials → Capital Structure Details]. But rates cut a second way that is not immaterial: the AED 71.5bn cash pile earns real finance income — AED 2.77bn sat inside the Real Estate segment result in FY2025 alone [FY2025 Annual Report, Note 3 — Segment Information, p.188] — so falling rates would cut that income more than they save on the group's tiny debt cost. The bigger channel is indirect and outside management's control: the AED peg means UAE mortgage and financing rates track US Federal Reserve policy, and the company's own auditor names "higher interest rates" and a "'higher for longer' interest rate sentiment" among the factors that "have increased the potential for constrained credit markets, negative capital value movements" in property markets [FY2025 Annual Report, Note 12 — Development Properties, valuation judgement, p.175]. |
| FX | Low | The dirham is pegged to the USD, and 93% of revenue is UAE (in practice mostly Dubai) [customer-geography §2]. The filing states plainly: "the AED is currently pegged to the USD, balances in USD and other currencies pegged against USD are not considered to represent significant currency risk" [FY2025 Annual Report, Note 34(b), p.215]. Residual risk sits in the roughly 7% international book (Egypt, India, Turkey): a +10% move in EGP or INR moves other comprehensive income (equity reserves, not the profit line) by AED 376.1m and AED 87.5m respectively (2025) [Note 34(b), p.216] — both small against AED 186.7bn total segment assets [segment-map §1]. Turkey is separately flagged as a hyperinflationary economy under IAS 29 [FY2025 Annual Report, Note 2 — Hyperinflationary Economies, p.174], a currency/accounting risk specific to that small unit. Second-order, unquantified channel: a weaker Indian rupee raises the AED price of Dubai property for Indian buyers, who are Emaar's single largest buyer nationality at 20% of sales [Q3 2025 Earnings Call Summary] — that effect shows up in demand, not in the FX note. |
| Government policy | High | Demand rests on Dubai-government levers Emaar does not set: population targets (Dubai's stated goal of 5.8m residents by 2040, up from just over 4m in 2025 [Q4 2025 Earnings Call Summary]), foreign freehold-ownership rules, and the Dubai Real Estate Sector Strategy 2033 and Economic Agenda D33 that the company itself cites as the backdrop for its growth plan [FY2025 Annual Report, Market Context section, p.19]. The Government of Dubai is also Emaar's largest shareholder, through Investment Corporation of Dubai (ICD) at 22.272% — the filing states ICD "is an entity owned by the Government of Dubai... which has a significant influence over the Company" [FY2025 Annual Report, related-party note, p.8717; Public Ownership Summary]. A reversal of the UAE's foreign-investor-friendly visa, ownership or infrastructure-spending policy would remove the demand engine this stock is priced on, and management has no vote over it. |
| Regulation | High | RERA (the Dubai Real Estate Regulatory Agency) governs off-plan sale structures and requires buyer instalments to be deposited into escrow — AED 42.9bn of Emaar's AED 52.6bn cash and cash equivalents at 31 December 2025 is customer-advance money sitting in escrow accounts, not free cash [FY2025 Annual Report, Note 10 — Cash and Cash Equivalents, p.~ (Note 10)]. Any change to escrow-release or off-plan rules would hit the funding model directly. On top, a new UAE Corporate Tax plus a Domestic Minimum Top-up Tax (DMTT — the OECD "Pillar Two" 15% jurisdictional minimum tax) was recognised for the first time at 31 December 2025: DMTT alone added AED 2,114,381 thousand (~AED 2.1bn) of tax in FY2025, and the quarterly tax charge jumped from about AED 70m in 4Q24 to about AED 1,234m in 4Q25 [FY2025 Annual Report, Note 2.4 and Income Statement; Q4 2025 Earnings Call Summary]. The tax rate and rules are set entirely by the state. |
| Weather | Low | Not disclosed as a driver of revenue or margin variance in the financial statements. Dubai's climate (heat, occasional flash flooding) is discussed only in the sustainability/ESG sections. Not proven from available data as a material earnings driver — dropped from further scoring beyond this note. |
| Geopolitics | High | The auditor's own key-audit-matter language on development-property valuation names "recent geopolitical events" and "current heightened geopolitical tensions" as sources of "greater volatility in property markets over the short-to-medium term" [FY2025 Annual Report, Note 12, p.175]. Dubai's buyer base is heavily international — the top five buyer nationalities are India (20%, the largest), UK, China, Pakistan and UAE nationals [Q3 2025 Earnings Call Summary] — and tourism demand is similarly international. Regional conflict, sanctions regimes, or a shift in safe-haven capital flows can swing Dubai property demand quickly in either direction, and management has no lever over any of it. |
| Consumer cycle | High | This is the core driver. About 80% of revenue is off-plan residential development recognised over time as construction progresses on already-sold units [business-identity §2; segment-map §1]; contracted pre-sales (AED 80.4bn FY2025) are the real leading indicator, and 80% of Emaar's buyers are first-time purchasers rather than repeat customers [Q3 2025 Earnings Call Summary]. A home or investment property is a discretionary, credit-and-confidence-sensitive purchase, so this swings hard with buyer sentiment, financing availability and the broader Dubai transaction cycle — a cycle that has both boomed and gone bust before (2009; 2015–2019), which is the relevant base rate for what happens to Emaar when sentiment turns, regardless of management quality. |
| Industrial cycle | Low | Emaar is not exposed to a corporate-capex or manufacturing order cycle the way an industrial supplier would be. The Leasing, Retail & Related segment (commercial and office space) is 15.5% of revenue [segment-map §1] and is influenced at the margin by office/retail-space demand, but the group's outcomes are set by residential/consumer and tourism demand, not industrial activity. Not scored further as a distinct driver. |

*Dropped as not materially applicable to a Dubai property developer and not scored further: Freight / logistics rates (Emaar has no disclosed freight or import-logistics cost line).*

## 2. Sensitivity, If Disclosed

Emaar publishes market-risk sensitivity tables in the FY2025 financial-instruments note. These cover **financial-instrument risk only** — they do not, and are not meant to, capture the Dubai property-demand exposure that actually drives the equity. All figures AED'000 [FY2025 Annual Report (IFRS), Notes to the Consolidated Financial Statements — Financial Risk Management, p.215–216].

| Variable | Disclosed Move | Disclosed Impact (2025) | Disclosed Impact (2024) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Interest rate (floating-rate positions, effect on profit before tax) | ±100 basis points | AED 26,165 | AED 29,875 |
| FX — EGP (effect on other comprehensive income) | +10% | AED 376,142 | AED 323,807 |
| FX — INR (effect on other comprehensive income) | +10% | AED 87,491 | AED 82,879 |
| FX — other currencies not pegged to USD (effect on other comprehensive income) | +10% | AED (45,607) | AED (43,560) |
| Equity price risk (investment portfolio, effect on equity) | +10% | AED 59,629 | AED 106,302 |

Context: AED 26m of interest-rate sensitivity against AED 25,656m FY2025 profit before tax is about 0.1% — immaterial [FY2025 Annual Report, Note 3 and Note 34(b)]. Every disclosed figure here is small relative to group scale (AED 186.7bn total segment assets). That is the point: the company's own quantified sensitivities are all tiny; the real dependency — Dubai property demand, government policy, geopolitics — is not something IFRS requires it to (or lets it) put a single sensitivity number against.

## 3. Classification

**Mostly externally driven.**

Strip the marketing layer and Emaar is a well-capitalised wrapper around the Dubai/UAE property cycle and the flow of foreign capital into Dubai real estate. About 80% of revenue is off-plan residential development and 93% of revenue is UAE — in practice almost entirely Dubai [segment-map §1–2; customer-geography §2]. The demand tap — buyer volumes, prices, absorption, foreign capital inflows — is set by the property cycle, population/visa/ownership policy, regional geopolitics and the new tax regime, none of which management controls. The company's own narrative anchors its results to Dubai population targets, government economic agendas (Strategy 2033 / Economic Agenda D33), and international buyer/visitor flows [FY2025 Annual Report, Market Context, p.19; Q3 2025 Earnings Call Summary].

This is not a pure pass-through, which is why the score below sits at the low end of its band rather than higher. Management holds real, sizeable buffers a commodity pass-through lacks: a contracted revenue backlog of ~AED 155bn (sold, not yet recognised as revenue — roughly three years of FY2025 revenue) [Q1 2026 Earnings Press Release; business-identity §2]; AED 42.9bn of buyer cash held in regulated escrow, released as construction hits milestones [FY2025 Annual Report, Note 10]; AED 61.7bn of net cash on a broad basis (netting in short-term deposits) against AED 9.8bn of total debt [FY2025 Annual Report, Financial Review, p.13]; and about 20% of revenue in steadier recurring mall and hospitality income [segment-map §1]. These buffer the near term and give management real levers over pricing, launch timing and cash conversion. They do not remove the cycle itself — they cushion Emaar's fall when it turns, not exempt it from turning.

## 4. External Dependency Risk Score

**62/100** — **INVERTED SCALE: higher = worse (more dangerous external dependence), per CLAUDE.md §12 and MODULE_RULES.**

Band 61–80: "Mostly externally driven, limited management levers." The score sits at the low end of that band because the disclosed financial-market risks (rates, FX) are genuinely immaterial and pull nothing up, and the contracted backlog, escrow cash, net-cash cushion and recurring-income share are real, quantified buffers that a pure commodity or FX pass-through does not have. But those buffers cushion timing; they do not change what actually sets the level of Emaar's future sales, prices and asset values — Dubai buyer demand, government population/visa/ownership policy, regional geopolitical stability, and a newly-imposed 15% minimum tax, none of which the company sets or controls. The 93%-and-rising UAE/Dubai revenue concentration [customer-geography §2] means these external variables are not diversified away: a single shock — a Dubai demand reversal, a regional geopolitical event, or a policy change on foreign ownership — would hit almost the entire business at once.

## 5. The Single Biggest Lever

Dubai residential property demand (buyer volumes, prices and off-plan absorption, driven by foreign-investor confidence, population growth and government ownership/visa policy) — a 20% adverse move here would cut new bookings and pressure the valuations behind the AED ~155bn revenue backlog far more than any commodity, interest-rate or FX move the company has actually quantified.
